question: Does Abandoned Hall's ability trigger if the spell is countered?
answer:
No. Abandoned Hall's ability triggers "when a player plays a spell," and a countered spell is not considered played.

A card is only played once the entire play process has finished in its entirety. [350.1] Abilities that trigger on playing a card fire when that act has been completed by the card's resolution; [419.4.a] if a game effect prevents resolution — for example because the spell was countered — the card is not considered to have been played and no abilities that trigger on playing cards fire. [419.4.a.1] This follows directly from what countering does: a countered card is cleared from the chain and is not considered to have been played. [425.1.b]

question: Can a unit moved into or away from Abandoned Hall by a spell be chosen?
answer:
Only if it is at Abandoned Hall after the spell fully resolves.

A card is only considered "played" once the entire play process has finished, [350.1] which for spells means after all instructions have been executed and the card is placed in the trash. Abandoned Hall's triggered ability therefore fires after the spell resolves, not when it is placed on the chain. [419.4.a] [383.2.c] By then, a unit moved into Abandoned Hall is present and can be chosen, while a unit moved away no longer qualifies as "a unit they control here."

question: Can a unit replayed here by a spell be chosen by Abandoned Hall's triggered ability?
answer:
Yes. Spells like Arcane Shift and Thrill of the Hunt add the unit to the chain as a pending item during their own resolution, pausing its play process while the spell continues. [354.2] [354.3] When the spell finishes resolving, it is fully played and Abandoned Hall's triggered ability becomes pending after the unit. [350.1] [419.4.a] [383.2.c] Because pending items are finalized in the order they were appended, [337.1.b] the unit is finalized and placed on the board first — resolving immediately on finalization [337.2] — before the triggered ability's target is chosen. By that point the unit is already present at Abandoned Hall and is a valid choice for the buff.

### Resolution Sequence [#replay-sequence]

Taking Arcane Shift as an example:

1. "Banish a friendly unit" — the unit leaves the board. 2. "then its owner plays it, ignoring its cost" — the unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [354.2] but its play process pauses while Arcane Shift continues resolving. [354.3] 3. Arcane Shift finishes resolving and is banished; the spell is now fully played, [350.1] so Abandoned Hall's triggered ability becomes pending after the unit. [419.4.a] [383.2.c] 4. Required cleanups run before either pending item can be finalized. [334.1] 5. Once those outstanding tasks are complete, pending items are finalized in the order they were appended. [337.1.b] The unit comes first, resolves immediately upon finalization, [337.2] and is placed at Abandoned Hall. 6. Abandoned Hall's triggered ability is finalized next; you choose a target, and the replayed unit is now present here as a valid choice.

question: If my Dazzling Aurora plays Akshan, Mischievous at the end of my turn, will the Dazzling Aurora I take from my opponent trigger that turn?
answer:
No — you gain control of it too late for it to trigger that turn. It can trigger at the end of your future turns for as long as you control it.

Dazzling Aurora's trigger condition is "At the end of your turn." "At" identifies a triggered ability keyed to a specific point in time during the turn sequence [383.1] — here, the Ending Step, when end-of-turn game effects take place. [317.1] [317.1.a] A trigger's condition is evaluated once, immediately after that point in time is reached [383.2.c] — it is not re-checked continuously for as long as the game remains in the Ending Phase.

Your Dazzling Aurora's end-of-turn ability plays Akshan after that point in the turn has been reached. After Akshan enters the board, his play effect is added to the chain as a pending item. [383.4.a] [383.4.a.2] You gain control of the enemy Dazzling Aurora only when that play effect later resolves.

At the end of your turn, Dazzling Aurora was still controlled by your opponent, so its controller-relative "your turn" condition did not refer to your turn. By the time you gain control of it, that point in the turn has passed; there's no second check waiting for it later in the phase.

This result is specific to Akshan being played by your Dazzling Aurora's end-of-turn ability. If you take control of an enemy Dazzling Aurora before the Ending Step, it triggers normally at the end of that turn.

question: If both players use Akshan, Mischievous to take the same gear, who controls it when either one dies?
answer:
While both Akshans remain on the board, the player whose Akshan took the gear most recently controls it. When one Akshan dies, the surviving Akshan's effect determines who controls the gear.

Each Akshan's play effect creates a delayed passive ability: "You control it until I leave the board." [390.4] [391] These abilities generate continuous effects that change the gear's controller — an inherent trait of every game object. [477.1] [477.1.a] Since both effects operate in the same layer and neither depends on the other, [478] they are ordered by timestamp: the earliest-established effect applies first, and the most recently established effect applies last, winning out. [480] [480.1] [480.3] Your opponent's Akshan was played after yours, so it carries the later timestamp — its control effect is the final one applied, and your opponent controls the gear.

When an Akshan leaves the board, its "until I leave the board" duration ends and its control effect ceases immediately. The remaining effects are then re-evaluated in timestamp order:

- **Your opponent's Akshan dies**: their effect ceases. Only your Akshan's effect remains, giving you control of the gear. - **Your Akshan dies**: your effect ceases. Your opponent's Akshan's effect was already the deciding one — they continue to control the gear unchanged. - **Both Akshans die**: both effects cease. Control reverts to your opponent, since it was their gear to begin with. If the gear is unattached and now finds itself in a base it doesn't belong to, it will be recalled to your opponent's base during the next cleanup. [323.7]

question: How are targets chosen when playing Alpha Strike?
answer:
When finalizing Alpha Strike on the chain, choose the friendly unit, then choose up to one enemy unit at a battlefield per point of its current might.

The friendly unit is chosen explicitly as a standard target. The enemy units are targets generated by the split-target instruction. [355.14.a] [355.14.b] [355.14.c] You may choose fewer enemy units than the friendly unit's current might, including zero. [355.14.c]

Since each chosen enemy unit is a target of Alpha Strike, is added as a mandatory additional cost for any of those units that have it during finalization. [356.2.a.2] [809.1.d]

All choices are locked in at finalization and cannot be changed after this step. [355.15]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You play Alpha Strike and choose a friendly unit with 4 might. You may then choose up to 4 enemy units at battlefields as the split targets. You choose 3. Those 3 units — and the friendly unit — are all locked in as targets. </Callout>

question: When is Alpha Strike's damage distribution decided?
answer:
The distribution of damage across the chosen enemy units is decided at resolution, not at finalization. [355.14.e]

The total damage available equals the friendly unit's effective might when Alpha Strike resolves — meaning any speed buffs or debuffs applied by either player between finalization and resolution will affect the damage pool. [359.3.f.2]

Each chosen target must receive at least 1 damage. [355.14.f] [355.14.g] Beyond that minimum, you may distribute the remaining damage among those targets however you choose, but all available damage must be distributed.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You chose 3 enemy units at finalization. When Alpha Strike resolves, your friendly unit has 6 might. You must assign at least 1 damage to each of the 3 targets. The remaining 3 damage can go wherever you choose — 4/1/1, 2/2/2, 1/1/4, and so on. </Callout>

question: What if the chosen friendly unit leaves the board or becomes illegal before Alpha Strike resolves?
answer:
It remains legal if it only moves to another board location while remaining a friendly unit; otherwise, Alpha Strike deals no damage.

Alpha Strike does not require the chosen friendly unit to be at a particular location. If it moves elsewhere on the board but remains a friendly unit, it is still a legal target and deals damage using its effective might when Alpha Strike resolves. [359.3.e.2] [359.3.f.2]

If the target changes to a non-board zone, stops being a unit, or stops being friendly, it is illegal as Alpha Strike resolves. [359.3.e.2] Alpha Strike still resolves, but the illegal target is unaffected and the "its Might" referent returns null, so the related damage instruction is ignored. [359.3.e.5] [359.3.e.12] [359.3.f.2.a]

question: What if my unit's might is reduced before Alpha Strike resolves?
answer:
If the friendly unit's might is reduced between finalization and resolution, the total damage pool shrinks accordingly. If the reduced might is now less than the number of chosen enemy unit targets, there is no longer enough damage to assign at least 1 to every target. In that case, you must drop the minimum number of targets such that the number of remaining targets equals the friendly unit's current might [355.14.h] — you cannot drop extra targets to concentrate damage on fewer units. [355.14.h.1]

Any effects triggered by choosing those units as targets remain triggered if the units later cease being targets. [355.14.i]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You chose 5 enemy units, targeting your friendly unit with 5 might. Before Alpha Strike resolves, your opponent plays a spell that reduces your unit's might by 2, leaving it at 3 might. You now have only 3 damage to distribute but 5 targets. You must drop 2 targets of your choice. The remaining 3 targets each receive at least 1 of the 3 available damage. </Callout>

<Callout type="warn" title="You cannot drop extra targets to concentrate damage"> You chose 3 enemy 1 might Recruits at finalization with a friendly 3 might unit. Before resolution, your opponent reduces your unit's might by 1 with Stupefy (leaving it at 2 might) and buffs one of their Recruits to 2 might with En Garde. You now have 2 damage to distribute but 3 targets. You must drop exactly 1 target — leaving 2 remaining targets that each receive at least 1 damage. You cannot drop 2 targets to leave only the 2 might Recruit and assign both damage to it. </Callout>

question: How does Aphelios, Exalted interact with Svellsongur and Shady Spectacles?
answer:
Aphelios triggers once when either Svellsongur or Shady Spectacles is attached to him. A different unit that becomes a copy of Aphelios through Shady Spectacles does not trigger.

<Callout type="info" title="Earlier Svellsongur ruling"> The January 2026 [Spiritforged FAQ](https://playriftbound.com/en-us/news/rules-and-releases/riftbound-spiritforged-faq/) ruled that Svellsongur copied Aphelios's ability in time for both instances to trigger. At the time, the FAQ noted that the copy system was not yet fully defined in the core rules. Guidance of this kind typically bridges gaps between core rules versions and is superseded when an updated Core Rules Document addresses the issue. Core Rules 1.4 now addresses this timing directly, so this page follows the current rules. </Callout>

Both equipment abilities are replacement effects because they describe an action that happens "as" the equipment is attached. [369.1] Each replaces the single attachment event with that same attachment event plus its copy action. [370.1.b.1] This does not create a second attachment event: events are simultaneous only when they result from the same game action, [370.1.a.2] and copying is a separate game action added to the attachment event by the replacement effect.

Aphelios's trigger condition is evaluated after the attachment event is processed. [383.2.c] At that point, he still has his printed ability, so the game adds one pending trigger to the chain before continuing the equipment's replacement effect and performing its copy action. [401.1] [401.2]

With Svellsongur, that pending trigger is created before Svellsongur copies Aphelios's effect text. The newly copied text does not look back and trigger from the attachment that already occurred, so there is no second trigger.

With Shady Spectacles attached to Aphelios, his trigger is similarly created before he becomes a copy of the chosen unit. If Shady Spectacles is instead attached to another unit and that unit becomes a copy of Aphelios, the unit did not have Aphelios's ability when the attachment event occurred, so it does not trigger at all. Treating either copy action as another attachment and triggering Aphelios twice is therefore not consistent with the current rules.

question: Can I use Arcane Shift to banish my only unit at a battlefield and replay it there?
answer:
Yes, as long as you control the battlefield.

When Arcane Shift resolves, the replayed unit sits on the chain as a pending item throughout the cleanup that follows. Because a chain exists, the turn is in a closed state, [309.1] and cleanup step 4 — which would make the battlefield uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [323.6] The battlefield stays controlled, and when the pending unit is finalized you can choose to replay it there. Attackers cannot replay their unit to the attacking battlefield because they never control it in the first place.

### Resolution Sequence [#replay-sequence]

When Arcane Shift resolves, the following happens:

1. "Banish a friendly unit" — the unit leaves the board. 2. "then its owner plays it, ignoring its cost" — the unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [354.2] but its play process pauses while Arcane Shift continues resolving. [354.3] 3. "Deal 3 to an enemy unit" and "Banish this" both resolve. 4. Arcane Shift finishes resolving, queuing one or more cleanups as outstanding tasks. [321.1] 5. The cleanups run. The pending unit keeps the chain alive, so the turn remains in a closed state [309.1] and cleanup step 4 does not apply. [323.6] 6. Once all outstanding tasks are complete, the pending unit is finalized. [334.2] You choose where to play it, [355.2] and the battlefield is still under your control.

question: Does Astral Heron's ability trigger if it's your first card played to a battlefield this turn?
answer:
Yes — assuming it's played to a battlefield.

Play, in a trigger condition, refers to a card resolving, not merely being placed on the chain. [350.1] [419.4.a] Units resolve immediately after they finalize. [337.2] During that resolution, the unit becomes a game object, its passive abilities become active, and it enters the board at its chosen location. [359.2] [359.2.a] [359.2.c]

A trigger's condition is evaluated after a potentially inciting event has been processed, and nothing requires that event to have been caused by a *different* card. [383.2.c] [383.2.c.1] "When you play your first card each turn" begins the trigger condition, [383.2.a] and "if I'm at a battlefield" immediately follows it, so that additional requirement is also part of the trigger condition and is checked when the condition is fulfilled. [383.2.a.1] After Astral Heron finishes resolving, play-trigger conditions are evaluated. [419.4.a] If it's the first card played this turn, Astral Heron is already at the battlefield when its condition is checked, so its ability is placed on the chain.

question: Does Astral Heron trigger if your first card moves it to base?
answer:
No. If a spell such as Flash or Emperor's Divide moves Astral Heron to base while resolving, Astral Heron is no longer at a battlefield when its trigger condition is checked.

A card is not considered played, and abilities that trigger from playing it are not evaluated, until that card finishes resolving. [350.1] [419.4.a] Astral Heron's trigger condition is therefore checked only after the spell's movement instructions have been completed. [383.2.c] Because "if I'm at a battlefield" is part of that trigger condition, the ability is not placed on the chain if Astral Heron is at base by then. [383.2.a.1]

This differs from moving Astral Heron after its triggered ability has already been placed on the chain. At that point, the condition has already been satisfied.

question: Once Astral Heron's triggered ability is on the chain, can killing or moving it stop the cost reduction?
answer:
No. Once the triggered ability is on the chain, killing or moving Astral Heron does not stop the discount from applying to your next card.

"If I'm at a battlefield" is part of the trigger condition, so it's only checked when the triggering event occurs to decide whether the ability is placed on the chain — it is not re-checked when the ability later resolves. [383.2.a.1] Nothing in the effect references Astral Heron's location or continued presence, so removing it does not stop the trigger from creating the discount. Once created, that discount is a delayed ability and executes at its specified time regardless of whether Astral Heron remains on the board. [392]

question: If the spell that receives Astral Heron's discount is later countered, is the discount granted to a different card instead?
answer:
No — the discount is spent the moment it reduces that spell's cost.

Astral Heron's triggered ability resolves into a delayed passive ability, active only for "your next card" — a single specified window, not a standing effect. [390.4] [391] That window belongs to finalizing the next card, not to that card resolving successfully — it doesn't linger to see whether the spell goes on to succeed. Discounts are applied while determining a card's total cost, in step 3 of the play process, and the reduced cost is paid in step 4 — both steps happen well before the card is even finalized, let alone placed on the chain where it could be countered. [356.4] [356.4.a] [357] Whichever card is played next consumes that window the moment its cost is reduced; nothing that happens to that card afterward can reopen it.

A countered card does nothing and is not considered to have been played, [425.1.a] [425.1.b] and countering does not refund any costs paid to play it, additional costs included. [425.1.c] [425.1.c.1] That confirms the reduced cost itself stays spent — but Astral Heron's discount was already used up before the spell was even vulnerable to being countered, so there was never anything left to give to a different card.

question: If Azir, Sovereign is killed or returned to his base before his attack trigger resolves, do token units still move?
answer:
No. "This battlefield" is a referent: information drawn from the source of the ability itself. [359.3.f.1] Referents are checked at the moment the instruction executes, not when the trigger was placed on the chain. [359.3.f.2]

If Azir has been moved to his base or killed before the trigger resolves, there is no "this battlefield" to move token units to. The instruction cannot be followed and is ignored. [359.3.e.6]

"This battlefield" is not a target. It is programmatically determined from Azir's current location, since he can only ever be at one battlefield at a time — no choice is ever made. [355.10.d] [355.10.d.1]

<Callout type="info"> Two common plays that produce this outcome:

- Hidden Blade, when played from its facedown zone, can be used in response to Azir's attack trigger to kill him at speed. - Overzealous Fan's defend trigger fires simultaneously with Azir's attack trigger when combat designations are assigned. Because Azir's controller places their trigger first, Overzealous Fan's trigger sits above it on the chain and resolves first, potentially moving Azir to his base before his own trigger resolves. [464.2.e.1] </Callout>

question: Can my opponent react before Baited Hook kills my unit?
answer:
Yes. The friendly unit is selected as a target when the ability is finalized, then killed when the ability resolves.

"Kill a friendly unit" comes after the ":" in Baited Hook's activated ability, so it's the first instruction of the effect rather than part of the cost — an activated ability's cost is everything before the ":", and its effect is everything after. [377.1] Separately, that instruction selects a friendly unit and does not fall under a targeting exception, so the unit is a target chosen and declared during finalization. [355.7] [355.8] [355.10] This is the opposite of cards like Sacrifice, where "kill a friendly unit" is stated as an additional cost and is therefore excluded from targeting entirely. [355.10.c] [355.10.c.1]

After Baited Hook's ability is finalized, opponents have a normal opportunity to play Reactions before it resolves. [377.3.b.2] [406.4] Later in the same ability, "up to 1 more than the killed unit" references the unit affected by the earlier "kill" instruction, making the two linked instructions. [359.3.e.14] Because the unit has already moved to the trash by the time this later instruction checks it, the ability looks back at the unit's characteristics as they were immediately before it changed zones. [359.3.e.13]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You activate Baited Hook, targeting a friendly unit with 4 might. In response, your opponent plays Stupefy, reducing that unit's might by 1 down to 3. Stupefy fully resolves before Baited Hook's ability does, so the unit already has 3 might at the moment it's killed. When the ability checks the killed unit's might immediately after, it looks back at that same reduced value — so you may only banish a unit with might up to 4 from among the top 5 cards of your main deck, one lower than if Stupefy hadn't been played. </Callout>

question: What happens if the targeted unit is removed before Baited Hook's ability resolves?
answer:
The unit can't be killed, and no unit can be banished from the top 5, since nothing can satisfy a might comparison against a null value.

If the friendly unit is no longer a legal target when the ability resolves — for example, if it was returned to its owner's hand in response — it is unaffected by the ability's "kill" instruction. [359.3.e.2] [359.3.e.5] Because the unit was never killed, any information the ability checks about it, including its might, returns null. [359.3.e.12] "Banish a unit with might up to 1 more than the killed unit" can never be satisfied against a null might, so no unit can be chosen from among the top 5 cards, even though you still look at them. "Then recycle the rest" is unaffected by this, since it isn't tied to the killed unit's might — you still recycle every card you looked at that wasn't banished.

question: Does a unit's Deathknell resolve before or after the unit played by Baited Hook and its triggers?
answer:
After, even though it's finalized first — finalization proceeds in the order items were appended to the chain, but resolution proceeds in the opposite order, newest item first.

Baited Hook's ability resolves in its entirety without interruption, [354.3] so both the killed unit's trigger and the unit it later banishes and plays get appended to the chain as pending items during that same resolution, with the appended first. Once Baited Hook's ability finishes, those pending items are finalized in that same order — first — but the chain then resolves newest-first, so anything appended after the , including the played unit's play effect and any abilities triggered by it being played, resolves before it does. The step-by-step below spells this out.

### Resolution Sequence [#deathknell-order-sequence]

Killing Ruined Rex — whose reads "Deal 4 to an enemy unit" — as an example:

1. Baited Hook's ability resolves. "Kill a friendly unit" kills Ruined Rex. 2. Ruined Rex's trigger is added to the chain as a pending item, on top of Baited Hook's still-resolving ability. [428.1.a.1.b] [808.1.d.2] 3. Baited Hook's ability continues resolving: you look at the top 5 cards of your main deck and banish a unit with might up to 1 more than Ruined Rex's, then play it ignoring its cost. That unit is added to the chain as a second pending item, above the . [354.2] 4. "Then recycle the rest" executes, and Baited Hook's ability finishes resolving. 5. Two pending items remain: the and the banished unit. They must be finalized before anything can resolve, in the order they were appended — the first. [337.1] [337.1.b] Its target — the enemy unit to deal 4 to — is chosen now. [355.5] 6. The banished unit finalizes next, choosing its location, then resolves immediately by entering the board. [337.2] 7. If the banished unit has a triggered ability that fires when it's played, that ability is added to the chain now, above the , since it was appended later. [383.4.a.2] [340.3] 8. Once no pending items remain, the chain resolves top-down: [340.4] the banished unit's own trigger resolves first, and Ruined Rex's — appended before any of this — resolves last, dealing its 4 damage. [340.1]

question: If Baited Hook kills Glasc Mixologist and plays Karthus, Eternal, does Glasc Mixologist's Deathknell trigger twice?
answer:
No. Glasc Mixologist's has already triggered once by the time Karthus, Eternal enters the board.

When Baited Hook kills Glasc Mixologist, Glasc's is added to the chain as a pending item before he is moved to the trash. [428.1.a.1.b] [808.1.d.2] Baited Hook then continues resolving and may banish Karthus from among the top 5 cards and play him, placing him on the chain above Glasc's . [354.2]

Karthus enters the board before Glasc's resolves, but his passive ability is only active while he is on the board. [365.1] It was not active when Glasc's triggered, and by the time Karthus enters, that ability has already been finalized. Karthus entering the board does not cause it to trigger again. Glasc's resolves once, so it can play only one unit from the trash.

question: Does Baron Nashor move to the Baron Pit when it's created as part of playing him?
answer: No. Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit directly — his entry location is replaced, not his position on the board. A move is defined as a permanent changing position from one space on the board to another. [446.1] Baron Nashor is entering the board for the first time (a zone change), which is not a move. [446.2]

question: What happens after Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit?
answer:
A non-combat showdown opens during the resulting cleanup.

### Resolution Sequence [#baron-pit-showdown-sequence]

1. The Baron Pit is newly created and has no controller when Baron Nashor enters it. [439.4.b] 2. Baron Nashor entering the uncontrolled battlefield applies contested status to it. [190.3.a.1] 3. During the resulting cleanup, a non-combat showdown is marked as staged at the Baron Pit. [316.8.b] [323.8] 4. Later in that cleanup, the staged showdown opens. [323.12] [344.2]

If an opposing unit arrives at the Baron Pit during the showdown, a combat is staged and the non-combat showdown becomes a combat showdown during the following cleanup. [316.8.b.1.a] [323.9] [323.14]

If the showdown closes with only Baron Nashor's controller's units present at the Baron Pit, and they have not yet scored it this turn, they conquer it and score. [348.2.a] [348.2.a.1]

question: Does the Baron Pit need to be scored to win by conquering?
answer:
Yes. Winning by conquering at match point requires having scored every battlefield on the board that turn — including the Baron Pit. [471.1.b.1] If it hasn't been scored, the winning conquer draws a card instead.

Winning by hold is unaffected, as it has no such requirement. [471.1.a.1]

question: Can I play Baron Nashor while an opponent's Mageseeker Warden is at a battlefield?
answer:
It depends on whether the Baron Pit is already on the board.

**If the Baron Pit is not yet on the board**, Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit, not your base. As Baron Nashor is played, his "as you play me" instruction fires during the playing process — the Baron Pit battlefield token is added to the board. [135.2.b.3] [187.9] Under Mageseeker Warden's restriction, your base is the only valid playing location — where Baron Nashor is nominally played to — but his replacement effect overrides where he actually enters. [355.2.a] His "If you do, I enter there" then functions as a replacement effect that applies as he enters the board, replacing his entry at his original play location with entry at the Baron Pit. [369.3] [370.1.b]

**If the Baron Pit is already on the board**, the "as you play me" instruction does nothing — the Baron Pit token is only added if it's not there already — so the "If you do" condition is not met. Baron Nashor simply enters his base, the only valid playing location under Mageseeker Warden's restriction. [355.2.a]

question: Can Bone Skewer choose a unit that says it "can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities"?
answer:
Yes, as the untargetability is inactive in hand and hand cards cannot be targeted in any case.

Ruin Runner and Baron Nashor are made untargetable by passive abilities declaring that they can't be chosen by some category of spells and abilities. [757] [757.1] Passive abilities of permanents are typically active only while on the board. [365.1] Abilities that function in another zone self-describe that context, [366.1] which these untargetability abilities do not. They therefore have no effect while the unit is in hand. Beyond that, Bone Skewer never targets the chosen unit in the first place — cards in hand are never targets because the hand is not a public zone, [355.10.a] so there is no finalization step at which a unit there could be declared as a target. [355.5]

question: Does Bone Skewer stun a unit that can't be chosen by enemy spells or abilities?
answer:
Yes, because the reflexive trigger that stuns the unit does not ask its controller to choose anything.

If the opponent plays the unit, Bone Skewer's "then do this" wording creates a reflexive trigger as a pending item on the chain. [387.1] [387.2] [388.1] The trigger is linked to the preceding ability, and "it" can only refer to the unit played by that ability. [394.1] [397] When the trigger is finalized, no choice is made about which unit will be stunned; it is always and only that unit. Because the unit is programmatically determined rather than chosen, it is not a target. [355.10.d] [355.10.d.1]

This means untargetability — the "can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" passive on units like Ruin Runner and Baron Nashor — does not prevent the stun, since it only stops a unit from being chosen as a target and the stun targets nothing. [758] is similarly irrelevant, since is only added as a cost when a spell or ability chooses an opponent's permanent, [809.1.d] which is not the case here.

question: If a unit chosen by Bone Skewer has Hidden, can the opponent hide it instead of playing it?
answer:
No, hiding the unit does not fulfill Bone Skewer's instruction to play it.

Hide is a separate action, not a subset of play. [811.1.c.1] Even though the chosen unit is in hand and may have , Bone Skewer instructs the opponent to play it as a limited action. [419.3] That play follows the normal process unless Bone Skewer says otherwise, [419.3.b] so the unit is put on the chain and queued for finalization. [419.1] The opponent cannot choose to hide it instead.

question: Can a unit played for free by Bone Skewer still get an effect for paying an optional additional cost?
answer:
Yes, as declaring the intent to pay is what satisfies the condition, not the amount actually spent.

The phrase "any and all costs" in Bone Skewer's text is intentionally broader than the standard "ignoring its cost" wording. Standard cost-ignoring only zeroes out a card's base energy and power costs, [356.1.b.1] whereas "any and all costs" sets the card's total cost to zero, including non-standard costs like additional costs. [356.5.a] Despite this, the opponent may still declare their intention to pay an optional additional cost during step 2 of playing the card — the decision to pay is made before costs are determined. Once declared, that additional cost is folded into the total cost, which "any and all costs" then sets to zero, so it's already 0 when it comes time to pay. [356.5.a] An optional additional cost is considered paid based on the decision to pay, not the amount actually spent, [356.4.f.1] so the condition is fully satisfied. Any conditional effect tied to "if you paid the additional cost" therefore triggers normally.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You play Bone Skewer and choose Nami, Headstrong from your opponent's hand. Your opponent is instructed to play Nami to the chosen battlefield, ignoring any and all costs. As part of that process, they declare their intention to pay the optional additional cost of . That cost is already 0, so nothing is actually paid — but because they chose to pay it, the condition is met. Nami's triggered ability fires, stunning an enemy unit. </Callout>

question: Does Brynhir Thundersong stop cards already on the chain?
answer:
No. Once Brynhir Thundersong's play effect resolves, opponents cannot play further cards that turn, but cards already on the chain are unaffected.

To play a card means to place it on the chain and queue it for finalization. [419.1] A pending card has already been placed on the chain and queued for finalization, [329.1] [354.2] and a finalized card has progressed beyond that point. [329.3] Brynhir Thundersong therefore does not stop either from finalizing or resolving.

See also [What does "play" mean on a card?](/general-rules/playing-cards#play-definition).

question: Can I choose a unit's current battlefield as Call to Battle's destination?
answer:
No, because Call to Battle requires the player to choose the move destination, so the restriction on valid destinations applies directly.

When a spell or ability has the player choose a move destination, that destination must be somewhere other than the unit's current location. [355.4] [355.4.a] Call to Battle has the player choose both the unit and the battlefield, so the chosen battlefield cannot be the unit's current location. If no valid destination can be chosen for the selected unit, the spell cannot be finalized.

This contrasts with Flash, which specifies its destination — base — rather than requiring the player to choose one. Because no destination choice is made when playing Flash, this restriction never applies, and a unit already in base is a valid target.

question: When I play Consuming Curse from my trash, does it count itself for the bonus damage?
answer:
No. Playing Consuming Curse from your trash moves it onto the chain first, [354] [419.1] so it's no longer in your trash to be counted. Only the *other* copies still in your trash add bonus damage.

Shadow Assassin and Shadowblade Lurker work the same way.

question: Does Diana, Lunari's ability resolve before or after attack and defend abilities from the start of combat?
answer:
Diana's ability resolves after all attack and defend triggers generated as that combat opens.

When combat opens with a combat showdown, the attacker and defender designations are assigned to units. [464.2.c.3] Attack triggers fire when a unit gains the attacker designation, and defend triggers fire when a unit gains the defender designation. [383.4.e] [383.4.f] Those triggers are then added to the combat chain, with the attacking player placing theirs first, followed by others in turn order, and the defending player last. [464.2.e] [464.2.e.1]

Diana's "when a showdown begins here" trigger is a start-of-showdown effect, which the combat-opening sequence processes as its very first step — before designations are established and their attack and defend triggers are added to the chain. [464.2.b] Because the chain resolves newest-item-first, Diana's ability resolves last — after every attack and defend trigger from that same combat chain has already resolved. [340.1]

question: When do I pay the 1 energy for Diana, Lunari's ability?
answer:
You pay it while Diana's triggered ability is being finalized, before opponents can react.

<Callout type="warn" title="Outdated CR example"> Diana received a functional errata alongside the Core Rules 1.4 update. Older printings say "you may pay . If you do, ..."; her updated text says "you may pay to ..." instead. This changes the energy payment from an instruction performed during resolution into a cost paid while finalizing the ability. CR 444.2 still describes Diana using her pre-errata behavior and incorrectly places the payment on resolution. [444.2] </Callout>

Because "you may" is the first part of the effect, you choose whether to perform the ability during finalization. [383.3.a] The immediately following "pay to " is a cost within instructions, so the payment is treated as the triggered ability's base cost and must be paid for the ability to finalize. [383.3.b] [383.3.b.1] You may activate reactions while paying this cost. [444.2.c]

If you do not pay, the ability does not finalize and none of its effects occur. If you pay, the ability is placed on the chain; when it resolves, you , reveal the top card of your main deck, and draw that card if it is a spell.

question: When do I pay 1 energy and return a unit for Emperor's Dais?
answer:
You pay the energy and return the unit while the triggered ability is being finalized, before opponents can react.

<Callout type="info" title="Core Rules 1.4 errata"> Emperor's Dais received a functional errata alongside the Core Rules 1.4 update. Older printings separate "pay and return a unit" from "If you do, play a 2 Might Sand Soldier unit token"; its updated text joins them using "to" instead. This makes the energy payment and unit return parts of a single cost performed while finalizing the ability, so the unit can no longer be returned without also paying the energy. </Callout>

Because "you may" is the first part of the effect, you choose whether to perform the ability during finalization. [383.3.a] The immediately following "pay and return a unit ... to play" is a cost within instructions, so both actions form the triggered ability's base cost and must be completed for the ability to finalize. [383.3.b] [383.3.b.1] [404.1] You may activate reactions while paying the energy portion of this cost. [444.2.c]

Returning the unit is part of the cost, so that unit is not a target and returns to its owner's hand during finalization rather than resolution. [355.10.c.1] If you cannot or choose not to pay the entire cost, the ability does not finalize; you cannot return the unit without also paying the energy. [404.2] If you complete the cost, the ability is placed on the chain; when it resolves, you play a 2 Might Sand Soldier unit token at Emperor's Dais.

question: How long does Endless Riches make you skip your Draw Phase?
answer:
You skip every Draw Phase you would have for as long as Endless Riches remains on the board.

"Skip your Draw Phase" is a passive ability and a replacement effect that replaces your Draw Phase with nothing. [364.2] [443.1.a] Passive abilities of permanents become active when the permanent enters the board and are typically active only while it remains there. [359.2.a] [365.1] Once Endless Riches leaves the board, this ability is no longer active, so your later Draw Phases occur normally.

This is not a delayed ability that applies only to your next Draw Phase or only during a particular turn. Delayed abilities specify the window during which they apply, [390] but Endless Riches specifies no such window.

question: Where does a spell played by Fizz, Trickster or Kai'Sa, Evolutionary go while Endless Riches is in play?
answer:
It is recycled. The "then recycle it" text on Fizz, Trickster and Kai'Sa, Evolutionary creates a delayed replacement effect that replaces the spell leaving the chain with recycling it. [390.3.a] Endless Riches also creates a replacement effect that would replace the spell going to the trash with banishing it.

The result is the same regardless of the order in which the spell's controller applies these replacement effects. [372] If the delayed replacement is applied first, the spell is recycled instead of going to the trash, so Endless Riches no longer applies. If Endless Riches is applied first, the spell would be banished instead of going to the trash, but it is still leaving the chain, so the delayed replacement replaces that event with recycling it. [370.2]

question: Which costs does Ezreal reduce?
answer:
Ezreal reduces only optional additional costs you choose to pay. These costs use both the word "may" and the exact phrase "as an additional cost." [356.2.b.1] and are keyworded optional additional costs, so Ezreal reduces them too. [805.1.a] [820.1.d]

Ezreal's discount applies to the optional additional cost itself as soon as that cost is added, before discounts that apply to the card's total cost. [356.4.c] [356.4.d]

Mandatory additional costs are not optional because they omit "may," [356.2.a.1] and payments made while carrying out an effect are not additional costs to play that card. Ezreal does not reduce either kind of payment.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> Blast Corps Cadet says "You may pay as an additional cost to play me." Ezreal can reduce that optional additional cost to either or . By contrast, Ezreal does not reduce Cruel Patron's mandatory cost to kill a friendly unit or the an opponent may pay during Hard Bargain's effect. Ezreal does reduce Hard Bargain's separate cost. </Callout>

question: Does Fallen Feline stop a named spell already on the chain?
answer:
No. Fallen Feline prevents opponents from playing further spells with the chosen name while it is at a battlefield, but it does not affect spells already on the chain.

To play a card means to place it on the chain and queue it for finalization. [419.1] A pending spell has already been placed on the chain and queued for finalization, [329.1] [354.2] and a finalized spell has progressed beyond that point. [329.3] Fallen Feline therefore does not stop either from finalizing or resolving.

See also [What does "play" mean on a card?](/general-rules/playing-cards#play-definition).

question: Can Flash target a unit that is already in base?
answer:
Yes, because Flash specifies its destination rather than requiring the player to choose one.

When a spell or ability has the player choose a move destination, that destination must be somewhere other than the unit's current location. [355.4] [355.4.a] Flash, however, does not ask the player to choose a destination: the card specifies it as base. That step of the play process never occurs, so this restriction never applies.

The only choice the player makes when playing Flash is which friendly units to target. [355.5] A unit in base is a friendly unit and meets no other targeting restriction, so it is a valid target. [355.9.b]

When Flash resolves and instructs the game to move that unit to base, the instruction is impossible — a unit cannot move to its current location. Impossible instructions are ignored, and everything else resolves normally. [055]

Azir, Ascendant illustrates the same principle: its ability says "Move me to its location and it to my original location," where both destinations are derived from the game state rather than chosen by the player. Choosing a unit at Azir's current location is legal; the impossible swap is ignored at resolution.

question: If Gangplank, Naval replaces one part of a spell or ability, does the rest still resolve?
answer:
Yes. A replacement effect only replaces the specific event or instruction that qualifies for it. [370.1] For Gangplank, that means a stun, might decrease, or return to hand caused by a spell or ability that chose him.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> A player plays Star-Crossed, targeting their own Gangplank as the friendly unit and an opponent's Elder Dragon as the enemy unit.

Returning Elder Dragon doesn't choose Gangplank, so his replacement effect has nothing to apply to there — it's returned to hand as normal. Returning Gangplank is the qualifying event: instead of going to hand, he gets +3 might. The rest of Star-Crossed resolves normally; it simply produces a different result for the one instruction that involves Gangplank. </Callout>

question: What happens when Switcheroo would reduce an Empowered Gangplank, Naval's might?
answer:
The might reduction is replaced with +3 might, while the modifier applied to the other unit is unchanged. See [How does Switcheroo work?](/cards/switcheroo#might-swap) for why swapping creates two separate modifiers from a single calculated difference. [433.1.a] [433.1.b] Switcheroo chooses Gangplank when the spell is finalized, then creates one modifier for each unit when it resolves. If the modifier affecting Gangplank would decrease his might, that event is replaced with +3 might because it comes from a spell that chose him. If it would increase his might, it does not match the events his ability replaces and applies normally. The modifier affecting the other unit is unchanged, and the difference is not recalculated.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> An Gangplank at 6 might is swapped with a 1 might Determined Sentry at the same battlefield via Switcheroo.

The swap action calculates a difference of 5, then creates two modifiers: -5 might for Gangplank and +5 might for Determined Sentry. Gangplank's replacement effect intercedes on his -5 might modifier — decreasing his might is one of the events it replaces — and turns it into +3 might instead. The +5 might modifier applies only to Determined Sentry, so Gangplank's replacement effect does not affect it.

Gangplank ends at 9 might (6 base + 3); Determined Sentry ends at 6 might (1 base + 5). </Callout>

question: Can Glasc Mixologist's Deathknell target a unit that died from the same event?
answer:
Yes, because targets are not chosen until the ability is finalized — by which point all units that died in the same event are already in the trash.

Whenever a unit with dies, its trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item. [808.1.d.2] During a cleanup, this ordering is enforced system-wide: step 3a queues all triggers from every unit with lethal damage [323.4] and only then does step 3b move those units to the trash. [323.5]

The same result applies when one kill instruction kills multiple units. Their deaths are simultaneous because they result from the same game action, [370.1.a.2] and each relevant becomes pending before its unit moves to the trash. [428.1.a.1.b] [808.1.d.2]

In either case, all units that died from that event are in the trash before the pending ability is finalized and its target is chosen. [334.2] [355.8]

question: Can Glasc Mixologist's Deathknell play a unit to the battlefield where he died?
answer:
Yes, as long as you controlled that battlefield when Glasc Mixologist died.

**Outside a showdown**, the trigger remains on the chain as a pending item from the moment it is queued. Because a chain exists, the turn remains in a closed state, [309.1] and cleanup step 4 — which makes unoccupied battlefields uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [323.6] The battlefield stays under your control, so when the unit is finalized you can choose it as a valid destination. [355.2.a]

**During a showdown**, control of the battlefield cannot change until instructed by the steps of the combat or showdown, [190.4.b] so the question does not arise.

question: What happens when Glasc Mixologist is my only defender and his Deathknell plays a unit where he died?
answer:
Several things here commonly catch players off guard: surviving enemy units heal to full before the new unit arrives, neither player wins the original combat, and a second combat immediately follows.

The combat cleanup heals all units before any pending trigger can resolve, [466.1.a.1] [334] so by the time Glasc's finalizes and the new unit reaches the battlefield, the enemy is already back to full health. Because Glasc was your only defender, no defenders remain during cleanup step 3d, so the surviving attackers are not recalled. [466.1.a.2]

With units from both players now present, combat result is determined. Because both players have units there, the result is "No Result." [466.3.d] A fresh combat is immediately staged at that battlefield. [466.3.d.1]

question: If Heedless Resurrection is countered, is the killed unit returned?
answer:
No, as the kill is an additional cost and countering a spell never refunds costs already paid.

Killing a friendly unit is an additional cost required to play Heedless Resurrection. A countered spell does nothing and is cleared from the chain. [425.1.a] Countering does not refund any costs paid to play a card, including additional costs. [425.1.c] [425.1.c.1] That cost is paid before the spell resolves, so the killed unit is not returned.

question: Can I kill a unit with Heedless Resurrection's cost and then resurrect that same unit?
answer:
No, as the resurrection target must already be in your trash when you choose it, before the kill cost is paid.

When playing Heedless Resurrection, you must choose the unit to resurrect during step 2 of finalization — the "Make relevant choices" step. [355.5] At that point, the unit you intend to kill is still on the board, not yet in your trash. "A unit from your trash" must be in your trash to be a valid target, [355.9.a] so a living unit on the board cannot be chosen. The additional cost — killing a friendly unit — is paid in step 4, [357.2] after all choices are already locked in. [355.15]

question: Does Heedless Resurrection's "ignoring its cost" instruction also ignore the resurrected unit's additional costs, such as Accelerate?
answer:
No. "Ignoring its cost" only sets the resurrected unit's base energy and power costs to zero; additional costs are not waived.

When Heedless Resurrection instructs you to play a unit from your trash "ignoring its cost," that instruction sets the resurrected unit's base energy cost and base power cost to zero. [356.1.b.1] Additional costs — such as the optional cost — are applied in a separate step after the base cost is zeroed out and are unaffected by the "ignoring its cost" instruction. [356.1.b.3] If the resurrected unit has an optional additional cost you may choose whether to pay it; [356.2.b.1] if it has a mandatory additional cost you must pay it. [356.2.a.1]

question: If Heedless Resurrection gains Repeat, do I need to kill a friendly unit for each repetition?
answer:
No. The additional cost to kill a friendly unit is paid once, as part of playing the spell.

Additional costs like this are paid during step 4 of playing the card, [357.2] not during resolution. makes the spell's instructions execute an additional time upon resolution, [820.1.d.1] but does not re-run costs that were already paid while playing — "as you play me" instructions execute once, before the execution ever occurs. [135.2.b.3]

No matter how many times is paid, the spell is only played once, [820.3.a] so you kill only one friendly unit.

question: If Hidden Blade's kill is replaced, does the target's controller draw?
answer:
Yes. Replacing Hidden Blade's kill does not prevent its linked draw instruction from executing.

The phrase "its controller" links the draw to the unit affected by the preceding kill instruction. [359.3.e.14] Replacing that kill action does not stop the later linked instruction unless it directly references the action itself. [359.3.e.14.b] Hidden Blade's draw references the targeted unit's controller, not whether the unit was killed, so the draw still executes.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You play Hidden Blade targeting an opponent's unit. They respond with Zhonya's Hourglass, which replaces the unit's death. The unit is not killed. Because it was still a legal target when Hidden Blade resolved, the opponent draws 2. </Callout>

question: If Hidden Blade's target becomes illegal, does that target's controller draw?
answer:
No. An illegal target is entirely unaffected by the spell, and the draw is no exception.

An illegal target is unaffected by the spell, so Hidden Blade's kill instruction is ignored. [359.3.e.5] When an earlier linked instruction is ignored, its later linked instructions are also ignored, so the controller does not draw. [359.3.e.14.a]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You play Hidden Blade targeting an opponent's unit at a battlefield. They respond by moving it to their base using Flash. Hidden Blade resolves. The unit is no longer at a battlefield, so it is an illegal target. The unit is not killed and the opponent does not draw. </Callout>

question: If I target Irelia, Fervent with a spell or ability and it gets countered, does she still get +1 might?
answer:
Yes.

Irelia is chosen as a target during step 2 of playing the spell or ability — the "Make relevant choices" step. [355.5] [355.7] This happens before the spell or ability is finalized on the chain and before opponents have any opportunity to react. After the spell or ability finishes finalizing, her targeting effect is added to the chain as a pending item. [383.4.b.2] [383.4.b.3] That trigger is finalized before opponents receive an opportunity to react. [337.3] [337.4] The trigger is not contingent on the spell or ability that caused it successfully resolving. Countering the spell or ability only prevents it from resolving [425.1.a] — it has no bearing on Irelia's already-triggered ability.

<Callout type="info"> Blade Dancer works the same way. Her triggered ability reads "When you choose a friendly unit, you may exhaust me and pay to ready it." It ends up on the chain before the original spell can be countered. </Callout>

question: Does Blade Dancer's ability trigger Irelia, Fervent's +1 might?
answer:
Not from choosing — but she can still trigger from being readied if she was exhausted.

Blade Dancer does not choose a unit — it does not target. [355.10.d] [355.10.d.1] "It" in "ready it" deterministically refers back to the unit already identified as Blade Dancer's trigger condition, with no separate choice made by the player. Irelia's ability can only trigger from Blade Dancer if she was exhausted and is readied by it — and only through the readying half of her ability, not the choosing half. [415.1]

question: Does Irelia, Fervent get +1 might when she readies during the Awaken Phase?
answer:
Yes, but only if she was exhausted and actually transitions to the ready state.

During the Awaken Phase at the start of each turn, the turn player readies all game objects they control that are able to be readied. [315.1.b] Readying is the action of marking a game object as available for action. [415.1] If Irelia was exhausted, she transitions to ready and her trigger fires.

If she is already ready at the start of your turn, she cannot be readied again [415.1.b] — no readying event occurs and the trigger does not fire.

question: Does a Repeat spell targeting Irelia, Fervent for both instructions give her +1 might twice?
answer:
Yes, as choosing her for each instruction is a separate triggering event.

is functionally "execute the spell's instructions one additional time". [820.1.d] When the Repeat cost is paid, choices for both executions are made during the same "Make relevant choices" step of playing the card. [820.2] [820.2.a] Choosing Irelia for the first instruction and choosing her for the second target her twice. After the spell finalizes, her targeting effect is added to the chain as a pending item once for each targeting event. [383.4.b.2] [383.4.b.3]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You play Feral Strength and pay its cost, choosing Irelia for both instructions. After Feral Strength finalizes, Irelia's ability triggers twice — once per targeting event — and both triggers are added to the chain. When her triggers resolve, she receives +1 and +1 from her own ability. When the spell resolves, Irelia receives +2 and +2 from the spell's two instructions. That's +6 might total this turn. </Callout>

question: If I move Irresistible Faefolk to an open battlefield and pull an enemy unit there, who is the attacker?
answer:
You — the Irresistible Faefolk player — are the attacker.

When Irresistible Faefolk moves to an open (uncontrolled) battlefield, that move applies the contested status to the battlefield. [450] [190.3.a] Irresistible Faefolk's trigger resolves after the cleanup caused by its own move, moving the enemy unit to that battlefield. During the cleanup following the enemy unit's move, combat is staged because opposing units are now present at the contested battlefield. [319.8] [323.9] When combat opens, the attacker is defined as the player whose unit(s) applied the contested status. [464.2.c.1] That is you — the player who moved Irresistible Faefolk. The opponent whose unit was pulled in is the defender. [464.2.c.2]

question: If I play Irresistible Faefolk directly to a battlefield, does its ability trigger?
answer:
No — playing a unit to a battlefield is not a move, so the ability does not trigger.

A move is defined as a permanent changing its position from one location on the board to another. [446.1] Playing a card involves it entering the board from a non-board zone (such as your hand), which is a zone change, not a move. [446.2] Because Irresistible Faefolk's ability specifically triggers when it *moves* to a battlefield, playing it directly there does not satisfy that trigger condition.

question: If an opponent responds to my move trigger by removing Irresistible Faefolk from the battlefield, does the enemy unit still move?
answer:
Yes — the enemy unit still moves to that battlefield.

Irresistible Faefolk's trigger condition is moving to a battlefield, and "that battlefield" in the effect is a referent to the battlefield named in that trigger condition. Information referenced from a trigger condition is checked when the trigger condition is fulfilled, not when the ability resolves. [359.3.f.3] That means "that battlefield" was already fixed the moment Irresistible Faefolk moved there and placed the ability on the chain.

Suppose an opponent responds to the triggered ability by playing Gust (or similarly, Star-Crossed), targeting Irresistible Faefolk itself to return it to your hand. Irresistible Faefolk returns to your hand, but the triggered ability is unaffected — it's already an independent item on the chain, and the battlefield it references was fixed at trigger time. When it resolves, it moves an enemy unit to that battlefield, even though Irresistible Faefolk is no longer there.

This differs from information derived from an ability's source or targets, which is generally checked when the referencing instruction executes and may become unavailable before resolution. [359.3.f.1] [359.3.f.2]

question: Does Karthus, Eternal's ability apply if he dies from the same effect as the unit with Deathknell?
answer:
Yes, because triggers are always queued as pending items before the dying unit leaves the board.

Whenever a unit with is killed — whether by a kill effect or by lethal damage during cleanup — its trigger is added to the chain before the card is moved to the trash. [808.1.d.2] Karthus's passive is only active while he is on the board. [365.1] When one kill action kills Karthus and another unit simultaneously, as with The Ruination, Karthus is still present when that unit's triggers. [370.1.a.2] In the cleanup case this ordering is enforced explicitly: step 3a queues all triggers [323.4] before step 3b moves any of those units to the trash. [323.5]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You control Karthus and a friendly unit with . Your opponent plays The Ruination, which kills all units. Both are sent to the trash, but not before Karthus's ability doubles the trigger. </Callout>

question: Does a single Not So Fast counter both Deathknell triggers when Karthus, Eternal is on the board?
answer:
No. If both triggers are legal targets for Not So Fast, one copy can counter only one of them.

When a friendly unit with dies while Karthus is on the board, his ability causes that to trigger an additional time. Each trigger is added to the chain as its own independent pending item. [808.1.d.2] Not So Fast targets a single spell or ability, so each copy can counter only one trigger.

This applies only when the ability chooses one of your friendly units or gear. Otherwise, Not So Fast cannot target either trigger.

question: Can an opponent play a unit in reaction to Kha'Zix, Mutating Horror's trigger to prevent the effect?
answer:
No. Once Kha'Zix's ability is on the chain, adding more units cannot prevent it from resolving.

Kha'Zix's ability reads "When I attack or defend, if an enemy unit is alone here, give me +2 Might this turn and gain 2 XP." The "if" clause immediately follows the initial trigger clause, so it is part of the trigger condition. [383.2.a.1] The condition is evaluated once, when Kha'Zix gains the attacker or defender designation. [383.4.e.2.b] [383.4.f.2.b] If the enemy unit is alone then, the ability is placed on the chain and a later arrival cannot undo it. If the enemy unit is not alone then, the ability does not trigger even if another enemy unit is later removed.

<Callout type="info" title="Contrast: if the condition were at the end"> If Kha'Zix instead read "When I attack or defend, give me +2 Might this turn and gain 2 XP if an enemy unit is alone here," the "if" clause would come after the effect instruction rather than immediately after the trigger condition. In that case the "if" would be part of the effect rather than the trigger condition: the ability would go on the chain whenever Kha'Zix attacks or defends, regardless of whether an enemy unit is alone, and the condition would only be evaluated when it resolves. An opponent could then play a unit at reaction speed to ensure two units are present at resolution, preventing the +2 Might and the 2 XP. </Callout>

question: Can Kha'Zix, Mutating Horror trigger multiple times in the same turn?
answer:
Yes. The once-per-combat limit on attack and defend triggers applies to each combat individually, not to the entire turn, so Kha'Zix can gain +2 might and 2 XP once in each separate combat it participates in. [383.4.e.2.a] [383.4.f.2.a]

Each time Kha'Zix enters a new combat it gains its attacker or defender designation for the first time in that combat, which is what triggers the ability. There is no rule preventing a unit from participating in multiple combats per turn, and each combat is an independent instance with its own once-per-combat tracking.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> After Kha'Zix wins a combat and the state returns to neutral open, you can play Charm to pull a different enemy unit onto Kha'Zix's battlefield. That unit becoming present at a battlefield Kha'Zix's controller already controls applies contested status, staging a new, distinct combat. When that combat opens, Kha'Zix gains the defender designation for the first time in that combat. If the pulled unit is alone, the additional requirement in the trigger condition is satisfied and Kha'Zix triggers again. Playing additional Charms repeats this cycle for as long as enemy units and Charms are available. </Callout>

For more on how attack and defend triggers work per combat, see [When do attack/defend triggers happen?](/general-rules/showdowns#attack-defend-triggers).

question: Can Lacerate target a unit with more than 3 might?
answer:
Yes, Lacerate can target any otherwise legal unit, regardless of its might.

"Choose a unit" targets a unit, [355.7] [355.9.a] and adds no might-based targeting restriction — "unit" only identifies the category of game object being targeted. [355.9.a.1] The instruction to kill it "if it has 3 might or less" is not part of the target description at all — it's a condition checked on the effect itself as Lacerate resolves. This is unlike a card such as Gust, which reads "Return a unit at a battlefield with 3 might or less to its owner's hand" — there, "with 3 might or less" describes the target, so it's a genuine targeting restriction and only such units are valid choices. [355.9.b]

question: If my opponent targets my spell with Lilting Lullaby and I counter my own spell in response, can I still play spells?
answer:
Yes. Countering your own spell removes it from the chain, so Lilting Lullaby has no valid target when it resolves — and with nothing to counter, the linked restriction on playing spells is also ignored.

When you counter your own spell, it is cleared from the chain. [425.1.a] "Spell" in a targeting context refers to objects on the chain. [355.9.a.2] By the time Lilting Lullaby resolves, its target is no longer on the chain and no longer meets the targeting requirements — this is mistargeting. [359.3.e.2] [359.3.e.9]

Because all of Lilting Lullaby's first instruction's targets are now invalid, the "Counter a spell" instruction does not execute. [359.3.e.7]

"Counter a spell" and "Its controller can't play spells this turn" are linked instructions — the second references the controller of the spell from the first. Since the earlier linked instruction was ignored, the later one is ignored as well. [359.3.e.14.a]

question: Does Lotus Trap affect how much damage needs to be assigned in combat?
answer:
Yes. When damage is assigned in the combat damage step, a replacement effect that would apply to the resulting damage is considered to apply to the assignment instead, so Lotus Trap's doubling takes effect as damage is assigned — not only when it is dealt.

Assigning damage and dealing damage are still distinct steps. [465.2.c.1] [465.2.c.1.a] But the rules fold damage replacement effects into the assignment step: any replacement effect that would apply to the resulting damage is applied to the assignment. [465.2.c.5]

A unit must have lethal damage assigned to it in full before any remaining damage may be assigned elsewhere, [465.2.c.3] so the doubling changes how much of the attacker's damage the unit ties up. The assigning player picks the smallest raw amount that, once doubled, reaches lethal damage — for a 3 might unit under Lotus Trap, assigning 2 raw damage doubles to 4, so only 2 need be committed to kill it. [465.2.c.4.a] When damage is finally dealt it is not doubled again, since the doubling already happened during assignment. [465.2.d]

If more than one replacement effect applies to the unit — for example a prevent effect alongside Lotus Trap — the unit's controller chooses the order they apply during assignment, which can change the final assigned and dealt amounts. [465.2.c.5]

question: Can I use Lux, Crownguard's ability to pay for Hard Bargain?
answer:
No. Lux's ability can add energy to pay a spell's costs while that spell is being played, but it cannot supply the energy demanded by Hard Bargain.

Paying a spell's costs is part of the process of playing it. During that step, its controller can activate abilities that add resources to pay those costs. [357.1] [357.1.a] Once the spell is finalized on the chain, its costs have already been paid and opponents receive an opportunity to play reactions. [359.3.a] [359.3.c]

Hard Bargain's instruction, "Counter a spell unless its controller pays ," is executed later, when Hard Bargain resolves. [158.1] That payment is not a cost of playing the targeted spell. Although abilities that add resources can normally be activated whenever a spell or ability requires resources to be paid, Lux restricts her added energy to playing spells. [429.3] It therefore cannot be used for Hard Bargain's payment or for another payment required while a spell or ability resolves.

question: Can I banish and play Nocturne, Horrifying if Burn or Minefield puts it into my trash?
answer:
No. Neither nor Minefield instructs you to look at or reveal Nocturne.

<Callout type="warn" title="Rules citation needed"> "Look" is not yet defined as its own numbered action the way "reveal" is. The core rules consistently treat it as a parallel, explicitly-instructed action alongside reveal wherever both are mentioned, and this ruling relies on that pattern — an official update giving "look" its own definition would let this be cited directly. </Callout>

Nocturne's ability reads "As you look at or reveal me from the top of your deck, you may banish me. If you do, you may play me for ." The word "as" identifies this as a replacement effect that can apply only while the qualifying look or reveal event is being processed. [369.1] [370.1]

Reveal is a defined action, and a player may only reveal cards when a game effect specifically instructs them to. [424.1] [424.2] [424.2.a] "Look" does not have its own numbered definition yet; as the note above explains, treating it as an instructed-only action alongside reveal rests on intent rather than an explicit rule.

does neither of these — it puts cards from the top of your main deck directly into your trash, with no instruction to look at or reveal them. [440.1] Minefield's printed ability, "When you conquer here, put the top 2 cards of your Main Deck into your trash," likewise contains no look or reveal instruction. In either case, Nocturne becomes visible only after it reaches the trash, a public zone. [108.2.d]

question: How does Promising Future resolve?
answer:
Resolve it in two passes: first, players choose and banish their cards starting with the turn player; then, players queue those cards for play starting with the next player. Do not resolve each chosen card as soon as it is put on the chain.

### Resolution Sequence [#resolution-sequence]

1. Starting with the turn player and proceeding in turn order, each player looks at their top 5 cards, banishes one, then recycles the rest. [303.2.a] The cards already banished are public information, so each later player knows what the players before them chose. [108.6.e] 2. Starting with the next player and proceeding in turn order, each player puts their banished card on the chain as a pending item. This only queues the card for finalization; its play process pauses while Promising Future continues resolving. [354.2] [354.3] 3. Promising Future finishes resolving. At this point, Promising Future being played causes applicable abilities on cards such as Ravenbloom Student and Astral Heron to trigger. [419.4.a] Those triggered abilities are added to the chain after the chosen cards. 4. Finalize the chosen cards in the order they were put on the chain: the next player's card first, followed by each other player in turn order. [337.1.b] Promising Future ignores their energy costs, but their power costs and any applicable additional costs still apply. [356.1.b.2] If a player cannot pay all required costs, that card's play process is undone and it returns to banishment. [358.2] [358.5] 5. A unit or gear resolves immediately when it finalizes and enters the board. [337.2] If that permanent has its own play effect, or its entering causes any other abilities to trigger, add those triggered abilities to the end of the pending items already on the chain. [383.4.a.2] Continue finalizing the older pending items first, so every card chosen with Promising Future finalizes before any of those triggered abilities. 6. Once no pending items remain, players receive the normal opportunity to play reactions. After everyone passes, finalized spells and abilities resolve from newest to oldest. [340.1]

<Callout type="idea" title="In a two-player game">

The turn player chooses and banishes first, so their opponent knows that choice before making their own. The opponent then queues their card first, followed by the turn player. If both cards are permanents, the opponent's permanent enters first; if both are spells, the turn player's spell is newer on the chain and resolves first, after anything played or triggered above it.

</Callout>

question: Can a counterspell chosen with Promising Future counter another chosen card?
answer:
Yes, if the counterspell finalizes after an eligible spell or ability and has a legal target at that time.

Players only choose which card to banish during Promising Future's first pass. Targets for a counterspell are chosen later, when that counterspell is finalized. [355.5] A counterspell cannot finalize without a valid target; [355.8] if none exists, its play process is undone and the card returns to banishment. [358.5]

In a two-player game, if the turn player banishes a counterspell, their opponent sees that public choice before selecting their own card. The opponent's card is then queued and finalized first, followed by the turn player's counterspell. [337.1.b] If the opponent chose a spell that the counterspell can target, the turn player can choose it while finalizing their counterspell. The counterspell is newer on the chain and resolves first, allowing it to counter the opponent's spell before that spell resolves. [340.1]

The opponent can avoid this by choosing a permanent, a spell that cannot be countered, or a spell that does not meet that counterspell's targeting requirements. If this leaves the counterspell with no other legal target, it cannot be finalized. Conversely, a counterspell queued before another chosen card cannot wait for that later pending card to finalize; it needs an eligible target when its own targets are chosen.

question: Does Brynhir Thundersong stop an opponent's card chosen with Promising Future from being played?
answer:
Only if Brynhir Thundersong's play effect resolved before Promising Future instructs that opponent to play their chosen card. In that case, the instructed play is skipped as impossible and the chosen card remains banished. [358.3.a]

If Brynhir herself is chosen with Promising Future, she does not stop any of the other chosen cards. All chosen cards are already on the chain and queued for finalization before her play effect exists.

Promising Future puts each chosen card on the chain as a pending item while it resolves. [354.2] [354.3] Brynhir's play effect is only added as another pending item after she finalizes and enters the board. [383.4.a.2] The opponent's chosen card either finalized before Brynhir or is an older pending item, so it finalizes before her play effect in either ordering. [337.1.b]

If the opponent's card is a spell, Brynhir's play effect may resolve before that spell resolves, but it still does not stop the spell. As an instruction, "play" means putting a new card on the chain and queuing it for finalization; [419.1] it does not mean finalizing or resolving a card already there. Brynhir prevents opponents from starting that process for any further cards that turn, but she does not remove, counter, or prevent the resolution of cards already on the chain. See also [What does "play" mean on a card?](/general-rules/playing-cards#play-definition).

question: When Akshan, Mischievous is chosen with Promising Future, does he have to pay his additional cost before knowing whether he can take Dazzling Aurora?
answer:
No. Regardless of which card is banished first, Akshan's controller knows whether their opponent chose Dazzling Aurora before deciding whether to pay Akshan's additional cost, and his play effect can take control of it.

Akshan's controller decides whether to pay his optional additional cost while Akshan is being finalized, not when he is first banished or put on the chain. [355.1.a] His play effect is a separate pending ability added after Akshan finalizes and enters the board. [383.4.a.2] The enemy gear is chosen only when that triggered ability is finalized, rather than while Akshan himself is being finalized. [355.5.b]

This differs from a spell such as Salvage, which chooses a gear while Salvage itself is finalized. [355.5] If Salvage is queued before Dazzling Aurora, it finalizes before Aurora enters the board and cannot choose it. Akshan's play effect is instead a separate, newer pending item, so all chosen cards finalize before that ability does. [337.1.b] [383.4.a.2]

### Dazzling Aurora Is Banished First [#aurora-first-sequence]

1. The turn player banishes Dazzling Aurora. Because banished cards are public, their opponent sees that choice before selecting Akshan from their own top 5 cards. [108.6.e] 2. Starting with the next player, Akshan is put on the chain first and Dazzling Aurora second. 3. Akshan finalizes first. His controller already knows Dazzling Aurora was selected and may choose to pay Akshan's additional cost, even though Dazzling Aurora is still pending. 4. Akshan enters the board, and his play effect is added as a pending item after Dazzling Aurora. 5. Dazzling Aurora is the older pending item, so it finalizes next and enters the board before Akshan's play effect is finalized. [337.1.b] [337.2] 6. Akshan's play effect then finalizes. Dazzling Aurora is now an enemy gear on the board and can be chosen, so the ability can resolve and take control of it.

### Akshan, Mischievous Is Banished First [#akshan-first-sequence]

This ordering is simpler: the opponent sees Akshan before choosing Dazzling Aurora, then Dazzling Aurora is queued and enters before Akshan is finalized. Akshan's controller therefore sees Dazzling Aurora already on the board when deciding whether to pay the additional cost.

question: Does Ruined Rex's Deathknell deal damage before or after units are healed at the end of combat?
answer:
After. The combat heal is part of the same cleanup that queues the trigger, and the trigger does not resolve until that cleanup has run to completion.

When Ruined Rex dies with lethal damage during a combat cleanup, the steps run in this order:

1. **Step 3a** — Ruined Rex's trigger is added to the chain as a pending item. [323.4] [808.1.d.2] 2. **Step 3b** — Ruined Rex is moved to the trash. [323.5] 3. **Step 3c** — All units are healed. This step is inserted by the combat special cleanup. [466.1.a.1]

The pending trigger does not begin finalization until the cleanup task is complete. [334] After the cleanup, the trigger is finalized and its target is chosen. Once no pending items remain, players receive priority before the trigger resolves. [337.4] If it is not countered, it eventually resolves and deals 4 damage to the chosen enemy unit.

question: Can Ruined Rex's Deathknell target the Mech tokens created by Ferrous Forerunner's Deathknell, if both die at the same time?
answer:
No. Ruined Rex chooses its target before Ferrous Forerunner creates its Mech tokens.

When both units die in the same cleanup, their abilities become pending items. [323.4] All pending items are finalized before players receive priority and ordinary abilities begin resolving. [337.3] [337.4]

Ruined Rex chooses its target during finalization, [355.5] while Ferrous Forerunner creates its Mechs only when its ability resolves. Regardless of finalization order, those Mechs do not exist when Rex chooses its target.

question: If Sacrifice is countered, is the killed unit returned?
answer:
No, as the kill is an additional cost and countering a spell never refunds costs already paid.

Killing a friendly unit is an additional cost required to play Sacrifice. A countered spell does nothing and is cleared from the chain. [425.1.a] Countering does not refund any costs paid to play a card, including additional costs. [425.1.c] [425.1.c.1] That cost is paid before the spell resolves, so the killed unit is not returned.

question: Can my opponent interact before the Mighty unit chosen for Sacrifice's additional cost is killed?
answer:
