No normal reaction window opens between choosing the unit and killing it.

The unit killed as a cost is not a target — objects referenced as part of a cost are explicitly excluded from targeting. [355.10.c]

Costs are paid during step 4 of finalization, and finalization does not pass priority. [357.2] [337.1.a] During that step, Sacrifice's controller may activate an eligible ability with when resources are required, even without priority. [357.1.a] [429.3] [429.3.a] This limited exception does not create a normal reaction window or permit an opponent to play a spell like Stupefy between choosing and killing the unit.

By the time a normal priority window opens, the cost has been paid and the unit is already in the trash.

question: Does the Deathknell of the unit killed as the cost resolve before Sacrifice draws and channels?
answer:
Yes. The kill is a non-standard additional cost, not a resolution instruction, so it happens during finalization. That puts the on top of Sacrifice on the chain, where it resolves first.

### Resolution Sequence [#deathknell-sequence]

1. Sacrifice's opening line — "as an additional cost to play this, kill a friendly unit" — is a cost, not a resolution instruction. [356.7] 2. Costs are paid in step 4 of the play process, before Sacrifice has finished being finalized. [357.2] 3. When a unit with is killed to pay that cost, its ability is added to the chain as a pending item before the unit moves to the trash. [428.1.a.1.b] [808.1.d.2] The chain now holds the above Sacrifice, which is still mid-finalization. 4. Sacrifice continues through step 5, the legality check, and step 6, becoming a finalized chain item. [359.3.a] 5. Because the is still pending, it completes its own finalization before play proceeds. [359.3.b] 6. Once both items are finalized, the chain resolves from the top down. The was added last, so it resolves first. 7. After the fully resolves, Sacrifice resolves, drawing 2 and channeling 1 rune exhausted.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You kill Rift Herald, whose reads "Play a unit from your hand to your base, ignoring its Energy cost," to pay Sacrifice's cost. The resolves first — you play a free unit from your pre-draw hand — then Sacrifice resolves and you draw 2 and channel 1 rune exhausted. </Callout>

question: Does Shadow Assassin count itself when I play it from my trash?
answer:
No. Playing Shadow Assassin from your trash moves it onto the chain first, [354] [419.1] so by the time it enters, it's no longer in your trash. It enters ready only if a *different* copy of it is still there.

Consuming Curse and Shadowblade Lurker work the same way.

question: When I play Shadowblade Lurker from my trash, does it discount its own cost?
answer:
No. Playing Shadowblade Lurker from your trash moves it onto the chain first, [354] [419.1] so it's no longer in your trash when its cost is worked out. Only the *other* copies still in your trash reduce the cost.

Consuming Curse and Shadow Assassin work the same way.

question: Does a Reflection token with Temporary lose Temporary after Shady Spectacles makes it a copy of a unit that doesn't have Temporary?
answer:
No. It keeps the keyword granted to it separately, even if Shady Spectacles makes it a copy of a unit without .

Deceiver and Mirror Image first play a Reflection token, then make it a copy, and then grant it . The keyword therefore comes from a separate effect rather than from the traits copied by the token.

Shady Spectacles' "becomes a copy of that unit" applies in the trait-altering layer, [477.1.b] [477.1.b.1] while the separate keyword grant applies afterward in the ability-altering layer. [477.2] [477.2.a] The rules' Reflection example likewise confirms that copied Reflection tokens retain . [477.1.b.1.b] Because the grant has no stated duration, it continues for as long as the token remains on the board. [801.3.a.3]

question: Can Guardian Angel, Zhonya's Hourglass, or Tactical Retreat save a unit from Smite?
answer:
Yes. These effects can prevent the banish because the unit's controller decides which replacement effect applies first and can apply their protective effect before Smite's.

Smite's "if it would die this turn, banish it instead" is a replacement effect. [369.1] So are each of the three protective effects, which all replace the event of a unit dying. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the controller of the affected unit decides the order they apply. [372]

If the unit's controller applies their protective effect first, the death event is fully replaced — the unit is healed, exhausted, and recalled, or an equipment dies in its place. [370.1.a.1] A replacement effect can only be applied once to an event, and to any events that replace it; [370.2] once the death event has been consumed, Smite's replacement effect has no qualifying event left to intercept, and the unit is not banished.

Conversely, if Smite's effect is applied first, the unit is banished. The protective effects each replace a "die" event — since banishment is not a subset of killing, [427.2.a] none of them can chain onto the resulting "banish" event.

question: Does Sunken Temple trigger if I conquer with a unit that is only Mighty due to Assault?
answer:
Yes, Sunken Temple will trigger even if the unit is only because of the bonus might it gained from . [807.1.c] [807.1.d.1]

Control is established and the conquer occurs [466.5.d] before attacker and defender designations are removed. [466.7.a] This means units still have their attacker designation — and therefore active — at the time the conquer trigger is evaluated. [708] [710]

question: How does Switcheroo work?
answer:
Switcheroo does not swap might values directly — it determines the difference in current might at resolution and applies +X/-X modifiers accordingly.

Switcheroo uses the Swap action, [433] which calculates the difference between the two units' current might, then applies a -X modifier to the higher might unit and a +X modifier to the lower might unit. Current might means the unit's total might at resolution time, including all active modifiers: equipment bonuses, battlefield passives, conditional abilities, and any other effects. The modifiers Switcheroo applies persist until end of turn.

question: Are existing equipment bonuses or passive effects counted again after Switcheroo resolves?
answer:
No. Equipment bonuses, battlefield passives, and conditional abilities are already factored into current might when Switcheroo resolves. New modifiers that begin applying after Switcheroo resolves still apply normally, but they do not change the modifiers Switcheroo already created.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> You have a unit with 2 base might and attached equipment granting +3 might, giving it 5 current might. Your opponent has a 1 might unit at the same battlefield. When Switcheroo resolves, it calculates a difference of 4 and applies -4 to your unit and +4 to your opponent's. Your unit ends up at 1 might; your opponent's at 5. The equipment bonus was already included in the calculation — you cannot reapply the +3 afterwards. </Callout>

question: What happens when equipment detaches or passives stop applying after Switcheroo?
answer:
The Switcheroo modifier persists until end of turn, but the equipment or passive bonus is removed independently — which can result in very low or negative might.

Each modifier is independent: when equipment detaches or a passive deactivates, only that specific bonus is removed; the Switcheroo modifier remains until end of turn.

### Equipment detaching [#equipment-detaching]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> Your unit has 2 base might and +3 from attached equipment (5 current might total). After swapping with a 1 might unit, Switcheroo applies -4 to your unit, leaving it at 1 might (2 base - 4 from Switcheroo + 3 from equipment). If the equipment later detaches, your unit loses the +3 bonus but keeps the -4 from Switcheroo, leaving it at -2 might. </Callout>

### Passives [#passive-effects-ending]

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> Trifarian War Camp grants units +1 might while they're present. Your 1 might unit (currently 2 with the battlefield bonus) swaps with your opponent's 6 might unit at the same battlefield. Switcheroo applies +4 to your unit and -4 to your opponent's, leaving your unit at 6 might (1 base + 4 from Switcheroo + 1 from War Camp). If it later moves away from War Camp, it loses the +1 and drops to 5 might — the +4 from Switcheroo stays until end of turn. </Callout>

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> Wuju Bladesman grants a friendly unit +2 might while it defends alone. Your 3 might unit is defending alone, making its current might 5 with Wuju's bonus, while your opponent's attacking unit has 1 might. Your opponent plays Switcheroo targeting both units. Switcheroo applies -4 to your defender and +4 to the attacker, leaving your defender at 1 might (3 base - 4 from Switcheroo + 2 from Wuju) and the attacker at 5 might (1 base + 4 from Switcheroo). Once Wuju's passive deactivates — when combat ends or another friendly unit joins the defense — your unit drops to -1 might. </Callout>

question: Can Switcheroo result in negative might?
answer:
Yes. When referenced by spells or abilities and when summing combat damage, negative might is treated as 0, but might increases and decreases use the actual negative value.

Units can end up with negative might when modifiers included in their current might at resolution are later removed. Units with might less than 0 are treated as having 0 might when referenced by spells and abilities, and when summing might to be assigned as damage in the Combat Damage Step. [143.2.b] Units with 0 or negative might do not automatically die — units are only killed during cleanup if they have lethal damage, meaning non-zero damage equal to or exceeding their might. [323.5] [142.4.b]

If a unit later gains additional might modifiers, they add to the actual negative value.

<Callout type="idea" title="Example"> A unit at -2 might is targeted with Punch First, which reads "Give a unit +5 Might this turn." The unit ends up with 3 might — the +5 modifier adds to the actual -2 value. </Callout>

question: Can Temporal Breach banish a unit at a different battlefield if played from Hidden?
answer:
No, when Temporal Breach is played from Hidden, the unit it banishes must be chosen from among units at the battlefield where it was hidden.

"Banish a unit" chooses a specific game object to affect, making it a target, declared as Temporal Breach is put on the chain. [355.5] [355.7] [355.8] Choices made while playing a card from Hidden are restricted to the battlefield where it was hidden. [811.1.d] Specifically, if a Hidden spell chooses any targets, those targets must be chosen from among options at that battlefield, unless the ability explicitly restricts targeting in a way that makes this impossible. [811.1.d.2] Temporal Breach's own wording doesn't restrict its target to a location, so this Hidden restriction applies in full — a unit at another battlefield, or in base, isn't a legal target when it's played from Hidden.

If Temporal Breach is played normally, the Hidden restriction does not apply. It may target an otherwise legal unit at any board location, including a base or battlefield. [811.3]

question: If the unit banished by Temporal Breach has Hidden, can its owner hide it instead of playing it?
answer:
No, hiding the unit does not fulfill Temporal Breach's instruction to play it.

Hide is a separate action, not a subset of play. [811.1.c.1] Playing the unit puts it on the chain and queues it for finalization, [419.1] whereas hiding would put it facedown at a battlefield. [421.1] Moreover, the unit is in banishment when its owner is instructed to play it, and only permits a card to be hidden from hand or the champion zone. [811.1.b] Hiding is therefore not an alternative to the instructed play.

question: Does a unit replayed by Temporal Breach keep temporary modifications or statuses?
answer:
No, the replayed unit does not keep temporary modifications or statuses it had before Temporal Breach banished it.

Banishment is a non-board zone, [056.1] and a game object that changes zones to or from a non-board zone becomes a new object for tracking purposes. [124] When the unit enters banishment, all temporary modifications and statuses on it are cleared. [124.1] This means effects such as Stupefy's might reduction no longer apply, and a unit that was is no longer when it is replayed. [124.2]

question: If Temporal Breach banishes and replays my only unit at a battlefield, can I score there on my opponent's turn?
answer:
No, as control of the battlefield is never lost during this sequence.

When Temporal Breach resolves, the replayed unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [354.2] with its play process held until the spell has fully resolved. [354.3] Once the spell finishes resolving, a cleanup runs — but the pending unit keeps the chain alive throughout it. [330] [331] Because the chain is not empty, the turn remains in a closed state, and cleanup step 4 — which would make the battlefield uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [190.4.c] [323.6] Control is never lost, so there is no opportunity to score a point. [469.1] When all outstanding tasks are complete, the pending unit is finalized [334.2] [337.1] and replayed to the same battlefield you still control, as dictated by Temporal Breach's own text. [359.2]

question: What happens if Temporal Breach banishes a unit at Rockfall Path?
answer:
Temporal Breach banishes the unit, but its owner cannot play it back to Rockfall Path. The unit remains in its owner's banishment.

Rockfall Path prevents the instructed play action. This does not stop Temporal Breach from resolving; when it reaches the replay instruction, that game action is skipped as impossible. [358.3.a] The earlier banish instruction is unaffected, so the unit remains banished.

question: What happens if Brynhir Thundersong prevents the owner of a unit banished by Temporal Breach from playing cards?
answer:
The unit remains banished.

If Brynhir Thundersong's play effect has resolved, opponents cannot play cards for the rest of that turn. Temporal Breach can still banish an opponent's unit, but that opponent cannot perform the instruction to play it back.

This does not stop Temporal Breach from resolving. The replay is an impossible game action and is skipped, [358.3.a] just as it is when Rockfall Path prevents the unit from being played to its previous location. Because the earlier banish instruction was completed normally, the unit remains in its owner's banishment.

question: What happens if Temporal Breach banishes a token unit?
answer:
The token stops existing the moment it's banished, so there's nothing left for its owner to replay.

Temporal Breach puts the token into its owner's banishment, which is a non-board zone. [056.1] Tokens can only exist on the board or the chain — if a token enters any other zone, it ceases to exist immediately upon arriving there. [186] [186.1] So by the time Temporal Breach's "then its owner plays it to the same location" instruction would apply, the token is already gone, and that part of the spell does nothing for it. [055]

question: Can I pay optional additional costs, like Accelerate, when replaying a unit banished by Temporal Breach?
answer:
Yes, since the replayed unit still goes through the complete, normal process of playing a card, and "ignoring its cost" only narrows one part of that process — the base cost — leaving everything else, including optional additional costs, unaffected.
